subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: attempting first, then asking for feedback [Action]
passage: Teacher's note, Shalini. Ankit brought his essay draft on Tuesday with a page of comments in the margin. He had written the whole first draft himself, then asked an AI tool two questions: which parts were unclear, and how the structure could be tighter. He did not paste in any of its sentences. The tool said his second paragraph jumped between two ideas, so he split it and rewrote both halves in his own words. He showed me both versions. The second draft was clearer, and, more importantly, he could explain why. I asked how he decided what to keep from the feedback, and he said he kept whatever made sense to him. I have told him that this order, own thinking first and feedback second, is a good habit for other subjects too.

qa.q: Which two questions did Ankit ask the tool?
qa.a: Ankit asked which parts were unclear and how the structure could be tighter.

qa.q: What might Ankit feel when he explains why the second draft is clearer?
qa.a: Ankit probably feels proud and confident, since he understands the changes as his own.

qa.q: What could Ankit do if the tool's feedback is confusing?
qa.a: Ankit could check with Shalini or a classmate, since a person who knows the assignment can say which comments to keep.

qa.q: How might Shalini see this way of working?
qa.a: Shalini sees own thinking first and feedback second as a good habit, and wants to encourage it in other subjects.

grounding: A student writes his own essay draft, then asks an AI what is unclear and how to improve the structure, and rewrites the text himself.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: attempting first, then asking for feedback [Action]
passage:
Wednesday
Finished my English essay draft, "Is a city a good place to grow up?", all by myself. 600 words. It felt messy.
Tejas said just paste the topic in and let the AI write a clean one. I didn't want that. It wouldn't be my argument.
So I pasted MY draft in and asked: "Which parts are unclear? How could the structure be better? Don't rewrite it." It said my second and fourth paragraphs made the same point, and my conclusion brought in a new idea, the metro, that belonged in the body. It also said my opening was a list, not a claim.
Annoying but true.
I moved the metro part up, merged paragraphs two and four, and wrote a new first line myself: "A city gives children more doors, but fewer trees."
Reading it now, it sounds like me, only clearer.
Santosh

qa.a: Is a city a good place to grow up?

qa.q: How did Santosh feel about the AI's comments?
qa.a: Santosh was a bit annoyed but accepted they were true, and ended up pleased that the essay still sounded like Santosh, only clearer.

qa.q: What else could Santosh try on the next essay?
qa.a: Santosh could make an outline before drafting and also ask a teacher or friend for feedback, so the advice doesn't all come from one tool.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Santosh's approach?
qa.a: Tejas suggested letting the AI write it, so the slower route may look like extra work to Tejas, though Santosh ends with an essay that is truly Santosh's own.

grounding: Shows a student writing an essay draft first, asking an AI what is unclear and how to structure it, and rewriting the text personally.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: attempting first, then asking for feedback [Action]
passage:
Reena: did you finish the physics lab report
Vikas: yes. wrote it myself first, then asked the AI for feedback
Reena: feedback how
Vikas: I pasted my draft and asked "what's unclear, don't rewrite it"
Reena: and?
Vikas: it said my method section skips how I measured the time. and my conclusion doesn't mention the error
Reena: ooh that's what Sir always cuts marks for
Vikas: exactly. so I rewrote those two parts myself. took 40 min
Reena: why not just let it fix them
Vikas: because then next lab I'd make the same mistakes. now I actually get why the error goes in the conclusion 🙂
Reena: ok I'm doing the same. draft first, then feedback
Vikas: and don't paste your name or roll number in it
Reena: noted 👍

qa.q: What did the AI say the method section skipped?
qa.a: It skips how Vikas measured the time.

qa.q: Why did Vikas choose to rewrite the parts personally?
qa.a: Vikas wanted to understand the mistakes rather than repeat them next lab, and is pleased to finally get why the error belongs in the conclusion.

qa.q: What else could Reena do after getting feedback?
qa.a: Reena could check the feedback against the teacher's marking points, since the AI's comments may not match exactly what Sir looks for.

qa.q: How might Reena see Vikas's method?
qa.a: Reena is convinced and decides to copy it, drafting first and asking for feedback after.

grounding: Illustrates a student drafting a lab report alone, asking an AI what is unclear, and rewriting the weak parts personally so the thinking improves.
